title: Pompey the Great
lead: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus, the Roman general who took Jerusalem in 63 BC, went into the Temple's holy place and made Judea pay tribute to Rome. The Bible never names him, but his conquest began the Roman rule that the New Testament takes for granted. The Psalms of Solomon mourn his capture of the city and, most scholars agree, describe his death on the shore of Egypt in 48 BC.

sections.b: Two Hasmonean brothers, Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, were fighting over the throne when Pompey came south from Damascus. Josephus tells how the party of Aristobulus seized the Temple mount and cut the bridge to the city, while the other party opened the gates and handed Pompey the city and the palace. Pompey built a ramp, brought battering rams from Tyre and broke into the Temple court; twelve thousand Jews died. He went into the Temple and saw what only the high priest might see, though he touched none of its treasure, and the next day he ordered it cleansed. He restored Hyrcanus as high priest, made Jerusalem pay tribute to the Romans, and took Aristobulus and his children to Rome (Josephus, Antiquities 14.4, sections 14.54–79). Tacitus says the same in a Roman's words: "by right of victory he went into the temple" (Histories of Tacitus 5:9).

sections.h: The dragon on the shore of Egypt (48 BC)
sections.b: Pompey lost the civil war to Julius Caesar and fled to Egypt. Plutarch tells how he was stabbed as his boat came to the shore; his killers cut off his head and threw his body out of the boat, and a freedman washed it in the sea and burned it on a pyre made from an old fishing boat (Plutarch, Pompey 79–80). The second Psalm of Solomon reaches its climax with the proud conqueror, "the dragon," pierced on the mountains of Egypt and his body carried on the waves with no one to bury him (Psalms of Solomon 2:29–31 in Swete's numbers). Gray, Toy and most scholars since read this as Pompey's death, which dates that psalm soon after 48 BC; Jongkind calls the identification with Pompey "now undisputed," and M. de Jonge, "although the language is traditional," sees "a reference to Pompey's death in Egypt in 48 BC." For the word "dragon" Gray compared Jeremiah 51:34, where Nebuchadnezzar "has swallowed me like a sea monster" (Jeremiah 51:34), a verse whose Greek has the same word, drakōn.

sections.h: Why he matters for the New Testament
sections.b: From Pompey's conquest on, Judea lived under Rome, first through Hasmonean and Herodian rulers and then through Roman governors. That is the world of the Gospels: the census of Caesar Augustus (Luke 2:1), the question of paying tax to Caesar (Mark 12:14–17), and the hope that God would give the kingdom back to Israel (Acts 1:6). The Psalms of Solomon, written by Jews who saw Pompey come, show how that hope looked in the first years of Roman rule: a son of David who would purge Jerusalem of the nations and of law-breakers (Psalms of Solomon 17:23–27 in Swete's numbers).
